@Sidharth Hariharan @Tito Sacchi @Auguste Poiroux re our discussion today of how the integrability stack relates to Gauss's approach -- below are some details from a GPT Pro conversation [that link isn't updating correctly at the moment due to a bug on openai's end; I'll try to fix it later, but all of the relevant content is below]:

Conceptually, old #229 proves a direct identity d = a'; Gauss reframes things as Fourier permutation identities of the six pieces.
In #229, the climax is still theorem d_eq_a : d r = a' r. In the Gauss branch, the main organizing theorem is instead that the Fourier transform permutes the I₁+I₂, I₃+I₄, I₅, I₆ pieces and hence a is a Fourier eigenfunction (eig_a). That is a real change in proof strategy, not merely a code cleanup. (GitHub)

How Gauss handled the MagicFunction.a.DoubleZeroes “integrability / sorry” spots

The short answer is: Gauss does not finish those exact lines in place. He replaces that whole local proof with a different contour-deformation setup. (GitHub)

In #229, the problematic spots are inside the two explicit Cauchy–Goursat lemmas cauchy_goursat_int_1 and cauchy_goursat_int_3. Both invoke an open-rectangle boundary-integral theorem, and after discharging regularity plus side-edge integrability by integrableOn_goal2/3/4/5, each proof still has a remaining sorry where the top horizontal edge must be shown to vanish as the rectangle height goes to infinity. The commented-out plan mentions a uniform_vanishing_topEdgeIntegrand argument and verticalIntegrandX, which matches the later ContourEndpoints / VerticalVanishing infrastructure. (GitHub)

Gauss replaces that with a three-step package:

First, it rewrites the real integrals as curve integrals on fixed segments:
I₁' and I₂' become curve integrals along the two left segments, while I₃'+I₄' becomes the sum of curve integrals along the two right segments. It also defines the Fourier-side integrand Φ₁_fourier and proves the Möbius/Jacobian relation Φ₁_fourier = (deriv mobiusInv) * Φ₃' ∘ mobiusInv. (GitHub)

Second, instead of sending the top side of bigger and bigger rectangles to infinity, it works in a fixed convex wedge domain wedgeSet whose closure only touches the real axis at 1. The key boundary fact is then localized: Gauss proves Φ₃' r → 0 as z → 1 within closure wedgeSet. That is the replacement for the old “uniform vanishing of the top edge” obligation. (GitHub)

Third, it packages the regularity needed for Poincaré/contour deformation as reusable lemmas: diffContOnCl_ω_wedgeSet and fderivWithin_ω_wedgeSet_symm. With those in hand, PermI12ContourMain invokes the generic assembled contour identity perm_I12_contour_mobiusInv_wedgeSet from the shared contour library, rather than proving a one-off open-rectangle identity for this file alone. (GitHub)

So the old missing obligations

  • “vertical sides are integrable,” and

  • “top edge vanishes as height → ∞”

get replaced by a different package of obligations:

  • segment-to-curve-integral rewrites,

  • endpoint behavior at the single closure point 1,

  • closed-one-form regularity on wedgeSet,

  • and generic contour identities under mobiusInv. (GitHub)

On the pure integrability side, Gauss also moves away from the old double-zero-specific files. The old split PRs used RealDecay, ContourEndpoints, VerticalIntegrability, and VerticalVanishing. Gauss instead introduces generic infrastructure like EndpointIntegrability for the endpoint weight (1/t^2)e^{-c/t}, and separate product-kernel integrability files for the Fourier-side arguments (PermI12FourierIntegrableI1, PermI12FourierIntegrableI2, PermI5Integrability). So the integrability work still exists, but it is now attached to the segment/Fourier kernel representation, not to the old vertical-ray/open-rectangle representation. (GitHub)

The cleanest mapping is:

  • old cauchy_goursat_int_1 / cauchy_goursat_int_3
    → Gauss PermI12Prelude + PermI12WedgeDomain + PermI12ContourAux + PermI12ContourMain (GitHub)

  • old ContourEndpoints / VerticalIntegrability / VerticalVanishing
    → Gauss WedgeSet, WedgeSetContour, EndpointIntegrability, and Fourier-kernel integrability modules (GitHub)

  • old direct endgame d_eq_a
    → Gauss perm_I₁_I₂, perm_I₅, then eig_a (GitHub)

My best read is that this is the real “difference in method”: the manual PRs were building a bespoke double-zero contour argument; Gauss dissolved that into a reusable contour/Fourier-permutation framework.

a few more ideas from GPT Pro:

My read: #229 is locally simpler; Gauss is architecturally cleaner. I would not say Gauss is better in every aspect. The old route is easier if your only goal is “finish the existing DoubleZeroes.lean proof with minimal conceptual change,” while the Gauss route is cleaner if your goal is “have a reusable contour/Fourier infrastructure in the codebase.” (GitHub)

Why #229 is locally simpler: it stays inside the existing proof story. DoubleZeroes.lean is a single 622-line file ending in the direct target theorem d_eq_a : d r = a' r, and the key unfinished point in cauchy_goursat_int_1 is literally marked as the ε–M “top edge vanishes” step, with a comment pointing to uniform_vanishing_topEdgeIntegrand. The Cameron PR stack was built exactly around that geometry: ContourEndpoints.lean adds verticalIntegrandX and uniform_vanishing_topEdgeIntegrand; VerticalIntegrability.lean proves the seven Prop. 4.4.6 integrability goals; VerticalVanishing.lean proves the needed Im(z) → ∞ vanishing lemmas. If you want the smallest perturbation to the old proof, that route is the shortest conceptual hop. (GitHub)

Why Gauss is cleaner as a final design: it breaks the argument into reusable layers with narrow jobs. PermI12Prelude says the plan is to rewrite I₁+I₂ and I₃+I₄ as curve integrals of the same holomorphic 1-form and apply Poincaré; PermI12WedgeDomain proves the only boundary limit it needs, namely Φ₃' r → 0 as z → 1 inside closure wedgeSet; PermI12ContourAux packages the closed-one-form hypotheses on wedgeSet; and WedgeSetContour factors out an assembled contour identity specialized to mobiusInv and wedgeSet, explicitly for both the J12 and I12 developments. That is a more general contour framework than the old “vertical rays plus a top edge at height T” setup. (GitHub)

So on the specific “simpler?” question, I would split it like this: for proving the theorem once, #229 is simpler; for maintaining the library, Gauss is simpler. The Gauss route is not shorter in raw code for this slice—its content is spread across several files such as PermI12Prelude (269 lines), PermI12ContourAux (83), WedgeSet (124), WedgeSetContour (198), and EndpointIntegrability (69)—but those files are shared-style infrastructure rather than one bespoke argument. That is usually the better trade once you care about reuse. (GitHub)

What from #229 should be preserved? Yes: some low-level analytic/library pieces. The strongest candidates are the pure real-analysis and Fubini/integrability modules, not the rectangle-at-infinity proof skeleton. RealDecay.lean was introduced as a top-level real-analysis helper with lemmas about exp(-c/t) and integrability near 0 / on infinite intervals; Integrability.lean gives Φ₁_integrableOn through Φ₆_integrableOn; and ProductIntegrability.lean adds product-integrand definitions, Fubini swap lemmas I₁_integral_swap through I₆_integral_swap, and a_integrable. Those are the kinds of facts that remain useful even if you abandon the old contour geometry. (GitHub)

What I would not preserve, unless you explicitly want a proof close to Prop. 4.4.6 for exposition, is the old bespoke vertical machinery as the main route: verticalIntegrandX, the seven named “goal” lemmas, and the whole “send the top horizontal edge to infinity” scaffold. That machinery is tightly tailored to one contour decomposition, whereas Gauss replaces it with a fixed wedge domain whose closure hits the real axis only at 1, plus a generic contour-identity layer under mobiusInv. That is cleaner and more portable. (GitHub)

One subtle exception is the old PhiBounds direction. In #229 there was a deliberate refactor to separate PhiBounds for modularity and even define it via explicit DivDiscBound constants, avoiding Classical.choose. That kind of interface can be worthwhile. But Gauss’s wedge-limit proof seems to bypass that bespoke bundle and call MagicFunction.PolyFourierCoeffBound.norm_φ₀_le directly when proving the boundary limit at 1. So I would preserve the actual bound theorems / computable constants if they are good library material, but not feel obligated to preserve the exact PhiBounds wrapper. (GitHub)

So my bottom line is:

  • Adopt Gauss’s proof architecture.

  • Salvage old generic lemmas.

  • Do not keep the old vertical/top-edge scaffold as the primary proof path unless you specifically want blueprint-nearness.

Sorry I couldn't make it to the packathon today - of course, I'm more than happy to help refactor #229 to follow what's best for the project. The GPT conversation above seems to consider all the contributions from #288, #296, #297 as part of #229, since #229 is rebased on top of Cameron's PRs. In fact, #229 includes only DoubleZeroes.lean, once you factor out all the changes from the underlying PR stack.
sorrys in #229 are still there because we have a too restrictive hypothesis in our formulation of Cauchy-Goursat - I remember discussing with Sid the possibility of importing a more general version from the PNT+ project. If Gauss has set up a more general and reusable architecture for this, it makes sense to use it.

(Yes, I asked about the earlier PRs in the stack, but it framed the answers in terms of spherepacking#229 because it has the rest of the stack. Also all of the PR numbers should be prefaced by spherepacking# rather than # -- sorry.)
